summary: Describes how the LZS compression algorithm is used with the IP Payload Compression Protocol. It is a companion to the DEFLATE document and specifies how LZS-compressed data is carried. It is informational and does not define an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo says how to compress the payload of an IP packet using the LZS algorithm, which shrinks data by replacing repeated stretches with short references to earlier parts of the same data. It also sets two rules that keep packets independent: the sender starts each packet with an empty history and sends everything it has compressed, so a packet can be unpacked without the packets before it.

subtitle: How the LZS compression algorithm carries a smaller IP payload, and the rules that keep each datagram readable on its own.

tldr.problem: The IP Payload Compression Protocol needs one specific compression algorithm, with a defined encoding and defined negotiation parameters, before an IP payload can be shrunk and carried.
tldr.mechanism: This memo applies the LZS algorithm, which keeps a 2,048-byte sliding window and replaces repeated data with short tokens. The sender resets the compression history and flushes the compressor for every datagram, so each datagram can be decompressed on its own.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational. It fixes the encoded format, the IPComp transform ID IPCOMP_LZS, and a 90-byte threshold below which compression may make a payload larger rather than smaller.

today: RFC 2395 is an Informational memo from December 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines a compression algorithm for the IP Payload Compression Protocol and says nothing about how widely IPComp itself was put into use.

sections.title: What This Memo Adds to IPComp
sections.content:
RFC 2395 defines how the LZS compression algorithm is applied to the payloads of IP datagrams. It is a companion to the IP Payload Compression Protocol, RFC 2393, which defines how lossless compression is applied to IP payloads in the first place. This memo supplies the algorithm and the parameters used to negotiate it; it does not restate the protocol.

The algorithm comes from Hi/fn, which developed LZS from a sliding window compression history similar to Lempel and Ziv's 1977 algorithm. LZS is a general purpose lossless algorithm that works with a wide variety of data types, and its encoding is efficient enough to compress strings as short as two octets in length.

On licensing, the memo states that Hi/fn holds patents on the LZS algorithm. Licences for a reference implementation are available for use in IPPCP, IPSec, TLS and PPP applications at no cost. Source and object licences are available on a non-discriminatory basis, and hardware implementations are also available.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP Payload Compression Protocol says how to compress a packet's contents, but it needs a specific algorithm to do it with. This memo names that algorithm, LZS, and says how the two negotiate it. The algorithm's owner, Hi/fn, holds patents on it and offers licences for a reference implementation at no cost.

sections.title: How LZS Compression Works
sections.content:
LZS is a general purpose lossless compression algorithm, developed by Hi/fn from a sliding window compression history similar to Lempel and Ziv's 1977 algorithm. Its encoding method is very efficient, providing compression for strings as short as two octets in length.

The algorithm uses a sliding window of 2,048 bytes. During compression, redundant sequences of data are replaced with tokens that represent those sequences. During decompression, the original sequences are substituted for the tokens in such a way that the original data is exactly recovered. That exact recovery is what separates LZS from lossy compression algorithms, such as those often used for video compression, which do not exactly reproduce the original data.

How much the data shrinks depends on the degree of redundancy in the original data. The memo's appendix measures this against the University of Calgary Text Compression Corpus, a set of 18 files with a total size of 3.278MB, and reports the compression ratio achieved at each datagram size. The measured ratio rises with the size of the datagram, from 1.18 at 64 bytes to 2.14 at 16384 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: LZS looks back over the previous 2,048 bytes of data. When it meets a stretch it has already seen, it writes a short token pointing at that stretch instead of writing the bytes again. On the other side, the receiver uses the token to copy the bytes back, so the data comes out exactly as it went in. The more repetitive the data is, the more the algorithm saves.

sections.title: Compressing and Decompressing a Datagram
sections.content:
Two rules govern what the sender does with each datagram, and both exist for the same reason: to keep datagrams independent of one another.

  • The sender MUST reset the compression history before processing each datagram's payload. This ensures that each datagram's payload can be decompressed independently of any other, as is needed when datagrams are received out of order.
  • The sender MUST flush the compressor each time it transmits a compressed datagram. Flushing means that all data going into the compressor is included in the output, so no data is held back in the hope of achieving better compression. Flushing is necessary to prevent a datagram's data from spilling over into a later datagram.

The input to the algorithm is an IP datagram payload, and the output is a new, and hopefully smaller, payload. The output payload holds the input payload's data in either compressed or uncompressed format, and the input and output payloads are each an integral number of bytes in length. If the uncompressed form is used, the output payload is identical to the input payload and the IPComp header is omitted. If the compressed form is used, the output payload is prepended with the IPComp header and encoded as the memo defines.

The receiver mirrors the sender. If the received datagram is compressed, the receiver MUST reset the decompression history before processing the datagram, and then decompresses the Payload Data field according to the encoding specified in section 3.2 of ANSI X3.241-1994. If the received datagram is not compressed, the receiver performs no decompression processing and the Payload Data field is ready for processing by the next protocol layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is compressed on its own. The sender empties its memory of earlier data before starting, and it sends everything it has compressed rather than holding some back for a better ratio later. That way the receiver can unpack a packet without needing the packets before it, so packets can arrive in any order.

sections.title: The Encoded Stream Format
sections.content:
The compressed stream is a sequence of compressed strings followed by an end marker. Each compressed string starts with a single bit that says what follows: a zero means the next item is a raw byte, and a one means the next item is a compressed reference. A compressed reference is an offset and a length. The offset is either 7 bits long or 11 bits long, told apart by a leading bit: a one gives a 7-bit offset, and a zero gives an 11-bit offset. The length is coded in a variable number of bits and covers the values 2 through 24.

The end marker is the bit sequence 110000000. A datagram payload compressed using LZS always ends with the last compressed data byte, also known as the end marker, and that marker is used to disambiguate padding. This allows trailing bits as well as trailing bytes to be considered padding. The size of a compressed payload MUST be in whole octet units.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressed data is a run of items, each either a literal byte or a reference to an earlier stretch, and it ends with a fixed marker of nine bits. The marker tells the receiver where the compressed data stops and the padding starts, so padding can be counted in bits rather than only in whole bytes.

sections.title: IPComp Association Parameters and Thresholds
sections.content:
Several parameters decide how LZS is used with IPComp.

  • Negotiation. ISAKMP MAY be used to negotiate the use of the LZS compression method to establish an IP Comp Association. The LZS Transform ID is IPCOMP_LZS, as specified in the Internet IP Security Domain of Interpretation, and this value is what negotiates the LZS compression algorithm under the ISAKMP protocol.
  • Other ISAKMP attributes. There are no other parameters required for LZS compression negotiated under ISAKMP.
  • Manual configuration. The CPI value IPCOMP_LZS is used for a manually configured IPComp Compression Association.
  • Minimum packet size threshold. As IPComp states, small packets may not compress well. Informal tests using the LZS algorithm over the Calgary Corpus data set show that the average payload size that may produce expanded data is approximately 90 bytes. Implementations may therefore not want to attempt to compress payloads smaller than 90 bytes.
  • Compressibility test. There is no adaptive algorithm embodied in the LZS algorithm for compressibility testing, as IPComp refers to.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ends can agree to use LZS: through ISAKMP, using the name IPCOMP_LZS, or by configuring it by hand with the same value. Beyond that, the memo gives one practical warning. A packet under about 90 bytes is likely to come out larger than it went in, so it is not worth compressing one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security section is one sentence long: it does not add any further security considerations beyond those that the IPComp specification has already declared. Everything about the security of compressed IP payloads is therefore left where IPComp put it.

The acknowledgements note that the LZS details presented here are similar to those in the PPP LZS-DCP Compression Protocol, so an implementation already handling that case has most of the work done. The authors also thank the participants of the IPPCP working group mailing list, whose discussion was working to generate the protocol specification for integrating compression with IP.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo adds nothing new about security. It leaves the question to the IP Payload Compression Protocol, which sets out the rules for compressed packets. It also notes that the format here is close to the one already used for compressing PPP links.
